DISSENT AND THE CHURCH. The celebration of the purchase of the chapel in Golborne-street, Werringtofl, by the Baptiste, took place on Tuesday everting. Tea was provided in the schoolroom, after which there was a public meetin* in the chapel. The meeting was presided over by Mr. G. McMinniea, J.P., and there were also present on the platform :—The Rev. A. Harrisdn, Mr. J. Smith. M.D., IP., the Rev. George Kennedy, and the Rev. J. Wilkinson, of Warrington. After devotional exercises, • Tir CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause. said . Ladies and gentlemen, I jvish in the first place to take this opportunity—the first that I have had—of congratulating this church and congregation upon that measure of success which has attended your re- ligious efforts, and which has enabled you to leave he chapel that you occupied in another part of the town, and occupy one much more commodious, and much mere convenient. (Applause.) I always see with pleasure the growth and prosperity of die- s smiting congregations, for several reasons which I shall not mention to-night, and for one which I shall men- t on. I have a belief, right or wrong, but still firmly held that that great mass of irreligion which lies outside all the churches has to be reformed and evane., geli,ed by the tree ctinrotfes of this country. (Ap- plans. ) I need sometime ago • a speech delivered by the Bishop of ltdancheer—you know that I have read mere than one speech by the Bishop of Manchester— ' (langhter)—but I read some time ago that speech in which he stated the number of Episcopal Churches in his diocese when he came, and the number of Churches that he had consecrated and opened. I cane not now give the figures. though I knew them at the time—(laughter)—but I can now give the fact, and the fact is this—that during the time that the Bishep of Manchester has occupied the position he holds in this diocese, the Church of England bee increased ex- actly in proportion to the population of the Church of England. It comes therefore to thie, that as an aggressive force upon the irreligion—as I said before— lying outside ell the churches, the Episeopal Church is altogether powerless. (Cheers.) It has held its own but has made no conquests, and I believe this is all you can expect from it, and all that you can get from it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The controversy in re- ference to Establishments is becoming so warm that most of the clergy who give the public utterances which we see in the newspapers, and especially most of the higher ranks of the clergy, devote a very considerable proportion of the speeches and sermons they make to this question of the Church as a State Establishment. The Rev. A. HAZEISON gave an account of the finan- cial position of the chapel, from which it appeared that the chapel was purchased for £760, and that a sum of £241 was spent on alterations, an dimprovements, making total sum of £991, towards which they had raised £732, leaving a balance owing of £259. A gentleman had promised to help them, but he had not said to what amount, but he said hat at least it would be £.50. (Cheers.) They would see that they were be- ginning already to remove it. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. Fairbank of Widnes, was prevented being present, as was also the Rev. Mr. Yonge, the newly appointed minister at Wycliffe, who was unfortunately indisposed. The Rev. J. WILKINSON said that in the matter of the Chairman they had got the right man in the right place. (Hear, hear.) His speech would prove that he was a commerciol man, and he acted like one. (Ap- plause.) If they did not take up his challenge he did not know what he would say to them, (a voice, We will.) There was an expression he had made use of which he much liked, and that was that the dissenters and Nonconformists had an advantage over the con- formists in one respect at least, that is to say that when they bought and paid_ for such a place as that, they could call it their own. (Cheers.) Parliament would have no control over them, and so far as they agreed amongst themselves they could have doctrines preached to their own liking. (Hear, hear.) Its the Established Church this was not so, the ministers could not preach as they thought proper, or ad as they would wish without being called before their betters to cease their doings. (Hear, hear.) Fortunately Dissenters had control over their ministers, and if they did not suit them they could give them what was vulgarity termed the "sack." (Laughter.) He wished them both temporal and spiritual improvement. (Cheers.)

Dr. Stfait said that he was very mnch struck by the opening remarks of the Chairman with respect to the privileges of Nonconforming bodies and the disadvan- tages under which th&Estabtished Church laboured as an aggressive force in the world. (Hear, hear.) He had been a warm supporter of the Liberation Society, as well as his friend the Chairman, and ever since he was a boy he had thought and felt sure that disestab- lishment was the best thing that could ever happen to the Church itself. (Cheers.) He had attended some special serf ces at the Manchester Cathedral, at which the hymns were Methodist and also the sermon. The place was aluiost crowded to suffocation, and the wor- shippers—who included those believing in all shades of religion—were most earnest in their devotions. (Hear, hear) That was a move in the right direction, and if all the clergy of the Church of England were engaged in that way, he believed they had a power for doing good more than that possessed by any Noncon- formist body in this country. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to give the Church a little more time— (laughter)—and he trusted that before long they would , find a great number of the ministers of the Church of England as devoted to Christ, and as anxious for their fellow-men as Dissenters were. (Cheers.) Might that time, which would be the brightest since the Reforma- tion, come soon. (Cheers.) It was the easiest thing in the world to get money. (Laughter.) They bought the iron chapel in Rylands-street, and transplanted it Ssnkey Bridges, where it was fixed. (Hear, hear.) They had spent nearly £3OO, which sum had come, and they had more than enough. (Cheers.) If they had faith in God, the money would be sure to come.

The R v. G. KENNEDY expressed the pleasure he felt at finding himself on the same platform as the Chairman. (Hear, hear.) Several of the email Bap- fist chapels had been the homes of the greatest evan- gelists who ever lived. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the Established Church, he said that he had never be- longed to it, and was born in Scotland when it was not in very good odour. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He felt that there was coming upon him as he grew older in England a hungering and thirsting for fresh air and elbow room, and he desired to have the windows smashed though painted with effigies of saints and martyrs. Whatever stood in his way, as a minister of a free christian religion, even when by law established, must break down. (Hear, hear.) He said of it as Lord Darby said to the people of England in reference to Constantinople, "I won't help to murder the Establishment, but I will not raise my finger te prevent it committing suicide." (Cheers.) The Itethodidlikad long occupied an invidious position politics /191 V (Hear, hear.) They had no politiosl standing, although they went in at the close of the conflict. and reaped the advantages that other churches had won for them at the hustings, whilst they had not moved their little finger to bring it about. (Cheers.) In all the conflicts in Warrington in the tirres4p come, for wresting the keys of the National Churchyards from the grasp of exclusiveness, for educstion, free from control of the State, in the important matter of a State paid clergy, and in all ether efforts for good and the concession of civil rights to all Christians, they would find him with them in heart and soul, and shoulder to shoulder, without fear, or flinching or courting the favour of any man. (Cheers.)

John Furey was charged with being drunk in Bridge-street early on Sunday morning, with assault- ing P.C. 18 (IdeClaren), and with diseharging a fire- arm, to wit, a revolver, at the entrance to Bridge- street Buildings, to the danger of the lives of passengers.—McClaren stated that he was on duty near Bridge-street Buildings, Bridge-street, about a quarter to one o'clock on Sunday morning, when he heard the report of a firearm. He turned round and saw the prisoner standing in the adjoining entry. Ha went up to him and asked him if he had fired off a firearm, when he replied that he had not. After some farther conversation had passed between them, the prisoner held the revolver, now produced, in front of his face. He had a severe struggle with the defendant, and at length managed to take the weapon from him. It was a six-chambered revolver. The prisoner then butted him in the face. He had the revolver in cue hand, and hold of the prisoner with the other, and in self-defence he was obliged to strike the man.—The prisoner was fined 40s. and costs.

div.p: THE ROBBERY AT THE FAIR.

Jane Fox was charged with being a person of sus- picious character, and with frequenting placas of public resort for an unlawful purpose, namely to com- mit a felony. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. It will be remembered that the prisoner was first brought before the Bench on Thursday, on suspicion of having stolen from the person of William Lowe, cattle dealer, about £4O in money. It was then stated that on Wednesday evening last, between six and seven o'clock, Mr. Lowe was in Bose-street, off Winwick-street, when he was accosted by a female dressed like the prisoner, who snatched a purse containing £4O out of his pocket. Shen then ran away but was subsequently apprehended and locked up. Mr. Lowe was now pre- sent, and stated that he could not identify the prisoner as the woman who stole the purse from him. This charge was, therefore, withdrawn, but for the other offence prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: SUNDAY TRADING PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: SUNDAY TRADING PROSECUTIONS.

Sarah Bate, butcher, Bridge-street, was summoned for having on the 2fith ult., "the same being the Lord's Day, commonly called Sunday, you, being then a butcher, and above the age of 14 years, did unlaw- fully do and exercise oertain worldly labour, business, and work in your ordinary calling of butcher upon the Lord's Day aforesaid, the same not being a work of necessity or charity."—Mr. Hunt said he received in- structions from the Watch Committee to suppress Sunday trading as far as possible. Last Sunday but one he deputed-Sergeant Berry to look into the matter and present a report, which he subsequently did. From the report it appeared that Mrs. Bate sold meat to four or five persons. He submitted the report to the Watch Committee, and they directed him to summon her as he had previously cautioned her. He might inform the Bench that up to yesterday 8 butchers, 73 provision shops, 11 greengrocers, 121 sweet and fruit, 10 barbers, and 11 tobacconists' shops were kept open on the Sun- day. Some of the shopkeepers said that if the drug- gists kept their shops open on the Sunday they would do the same. Mrs. Bate was a respectable woman ; and was not like some of the shopkeepers who were c3mplained about.—The Mayor said that there was no doubt that Sunday trading had grown to a very great extent in the borough, and frequent complaints had been made about the matter by respectable persons. Mrs. Bate's ease had been brought to the knowledge of the police, and, although ehe had been cautioned, she cmtinti, d to sell on the Sunday. That was setting the law at defiance to a certain extent, and the case be- came more flagrant on that account. They had as wish to be vindictive in the matter, but desired to put a stop to the wholesale trading on the Sunday, if pos- sible, so that the Lord's Day might be observed in the way it ought to be. In the present case the magis- trates had decided to simply inflict a penalty of be. without the costs, with the understanding, of course, that nothing of the sort occurred again. If other cases were brought before the Bench, such leniency would not be shown.—Mr. Hunt : Allow me to add that the persons, who purchase are liable to be summoned, but the Watch Committee directed that they should not be in this instance. A DRUNKEN BTABLISHMENF.

John Wycherley, of the Ride Volunteer public. house, Cockhedge-laue, was summoned for having on the 30th ult., being the holder of a license authorising him to sell intoxicating liquors, Bold a certain quantity of .the same during prohibited hours. He was also charged with permitting drunkenness. Inspector Singleton stated that on Wednesday night, the 29th ult., from information received from the Chief Con- stable, he visited the defendant's house, accompanied by P.C. Seed, about a quarter to twelve o'clock. They were accompanied by Phcebe Porter, a married woman. After some delay he was admitted, and inside the bar they found a man named Porter, who was drunk, lying down among some bottles. He went into the kitchen, where he saw the defendant and his wife, two young women who lived in the house, and a girl named Hickey. Hickey was drunk, and was subsequently fined by the magistrates for this offence. Hickey afterwards told the defendant to his face that Porter paid for glasses round after closing time. He (Single- ton) did not say that the house was a bad one, P.C. Seed gave corroborative evidence. Eliza Hickey said she remembered Inspector Singleton coming to the defendant's house on the morning in question. Not a drop of beer was drunk after eleven o'clock. Porter had supper at the house, and paid for drinks round be- fore eleven o'clock. Hickey and Porter were sober. In defence it was urged that there was no evidence to show that liquor had been sold during prohibited hours, and the rase must, therefore, fall to the ground. The Mayor : That case will be dismissed. As to the charge of permitting drunkenness it was stated that Porter went to Dr. Cannell, of Academy-street, at 1.46 the same morning, and he gave a certificate to the effect that the man was then sober. Mr. Wyoherley had been a public-house manager for ten years, and had never been complained of before. He called the wife of the defendant, who stated that neither Porter nor Hickey were drunk. Elizabeth Hazeldine cor- roborated this statement, and added that ,Porter' who was lame, fell down, and being without his crutch, was unable to rise before the police came into the house and saw him. Dr. Cannell stated that Porter came to him at 1.45 on the morning in question, and he treated him for a blow he had received over one of his eyes. He was then perfectly sober. Winifred Duffy stated that no drink was served after eleven o'clock. Neither Porter nor Hickey were drunk. The Mayor said they thought the charge of permittin drunkenness had been proved, and defendant would be fined £5 and costs. The money was paid. Porter was then charged with being drunk on the premises and also with being there during unlawful hours, and was fined 6s. and costs.

At the Petty Sessions, en Monday, a respectably attired man, apparent'y about 50 years of age, was charged with having wilfully broken a large number of windows in Church-street, Altrincham, that morn- ing. Previous to the hearing of the case the prisoner attempted to leave the court, bat was prevented. Superintendent Aston stated that the prisoner was brought to the Police Station that morning by Mr. Okell, an old resident of Altrincham, who had appre- hended him on the charge of breaking windows in Church-etreet. At John Worthington's one square had been broken, at James Stafford's two, at Worth- ington's three, atldies Mackei.zie's two, st John Ptigh's one, at Keleall'e two, at Wild's one value 165., and at Mr. Royle's two, value 7s. 6d. The defendant stated that he was a superannuated policeman from Manches- ter, and he should be glad if the Beech would adjourn the case so that he might make inquiries. The pri- soner, who was sober, said that he simply came out for a walk. He imagined that there was something wrong with him. Matthew Okell stated that his wife heard some man talking to himself, and upon going to the window she saw him "up with his stick and break a big square." She got witneos up and said, "Matthew, there is a man walking up toe street breaking windows." He slipped his trousers on and followed the prisoner, and saw him breaking windows. He missed him at the corner of the Market-place for a minute, and then saw the prisoner come from behind the " big tree." He asked witness what he was looking for, when he told him he wanted a policeman. Prisoner then said, "I'm a policeman." He followed prisoner towards the police office and then "collared" him and milled out "Lichee." The prisoner then began to strike him with his stick. On being asked whether he desired to ask the Witness any questions, the prisoner said, "it is no use staking him any questions, I say it was not me that did it, he is mistaken altogether." Okell said that he was sure he was the man. Prisoner.—l cannot say anything in this matter. I came from Manchester, where I am an ironmonger In Medlock-street, Hulme. I have been in the police and have a superannuation. I left at ave o'clock for a walk. Superintendent Aston.—l received him at twenty minutes to four. The prisoner was remanded until Tuesday, when his friends appeared and offered to pay the damages, whereupon the offender was discharged.

ATTEMPTED HIGHWAY ROBBERY IN DUNHAM PARK.

Ann Owen, a cook in the employ of Mr. Robert Platt, of Dunham Hall, having been to Altrincham, was re- turning home through the Park a few nights ago, when a man came out of a wood,—having in his hand a huge stick—and demanded her money. She told him that she had none, whereupon he attacked her with the stick, threatened to cut her throat, and tore her bonnet off. The poor creature cried for assistance, and a man named Taylor came up. The ruffian made off into the wood and was not again seen. A weak. minded man named James .Wright, of Police-street, Altrincham, was arrested and brought before the Altrincham magistrates on Fliday, but the woman who was assaulted could not identify him, and he was discharged.
A MAN KILLED AT WEST TIAIPERLEY STATION.

Robt. Martin, of Liverpool, was killed on Monday afternoon, near West Timperley. The deceased, who was 24 years of age, was employed as a temporary shunter, and was last seen alive by a man namedßrooks, about half-past three at Skelton Junction, when he took his lamp to light the distance signal. Ii conse- quence of that signal not being lighted, a man named Gibbous was sent about six o'clock to ascertain the cause. He found the deceased close to the signal dead. His skull had evidently been fractured by a passing train, and his brains were scattered about in all direc- tions. P.C. Harrington, who was sent for, searched the body, but found nothing in the pockets but a bunch of keys, and a letter, applying for a situation in the Lancashire Constabulary. The body was removed to the Pelican Inn, Timperley. Au inq test was held on Thursday, before Mr. Dunstan, coroner, when a ver- dict of accidental death WAS returned.

At the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, the above case came on for hearing. It was an action arising out of the disputed valifity of a deed of gift under which the defendant held certain land and buildings at Altrincham, of which property the plaintiff sought to obtain posseadon. Mr. Addison appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Ambrose, QC., and Air.ly were counsel for the defendant.

The plaintiff's case was to the afoot that during the present and part of the last century the family of Starkey canted on business as cabinet makers at Altrincham. Arthur William Starkey, by whom the deed in question was executed, succeeded to the busi- ness in 1856, and at that time he purchased from the Earl of Stamford and Warrington it plot of land upon which he erected some works, that were now valued at from £6,000t016,000. He bad ihhis employ an appren- tice named Nield, to whom he gave some shares in the business. Arthur William Starkey died on the 26th November, 1863, and for some time prior to his death he was in failing health, both bodily and mentally. The deceased had expressed his iutention to different relatives of leaving his property to his widow, who was livicg in the house with Nield, and they made no attempt to disturb her. She died 1872, and the plain- tiff, who as the grandchild of the founder of the busi- ness, as who, heir-at-law, then made a claim to the pro- petty. The defendant Meld, however' declined to give it up, and stated that on the 19th November of tne year in which he died Arthur William Starkey ex- ecuted a deed of gift, by which he made over the pro- perty to Null. As that proceeding was contrary b what the deceased had always expressed his intention of doing, the plaintiff and other re- latives were much astonished. They now con- tended that for a week before his death the de- ceased was suffering from delirium tremens, and was not in a condition to execute such a deed as that by which the defendant alleged he had come into posses- sion of the property. A number of witnesses were called in support of the Btatemeut of counsel. In cross-examination, however, they said they were unable to swear that the signature to the deed of gift, which was produced, was in the writing of the deceased Starkey. It waa stated by one witness that she nad been given to understand that the defendant Nield was to pay the widow of the deceased the BUM of £2 per week. . _ _
The Judge said that unless Mr. Addison could pro- duce evidence which would impeach or disprove the validity of tha deed of gift, it was udeless to occupy the time of the Court.
Mr. Addison said he ,had a number of witnessee, poor relatives of the deceased, who felt aggrieved, but their story would be about the same as that told by the wit- noses who had been examined.
Judgment was entered for the defendant, with costs.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL FALL OF AN ALTRINOHAM PAINTER.
div.p: THE FRIGHTFUL FALL OF AN ALTRINOHAM PAINTER.

It will be in the recollection of our readers that the other week Mr. Mates, painter, of George-street, Al- trincham, met with a serious and what has since prove I a fatal accident. Mr. Mates was painting the front of Mr. Wood's premises in George-street, Altrincham, over the clock, when the pony belonging to Mr. Wood suddenly started, and the cart wheel came in contact with the bottom of the ladder and brought the ladder and the deceased to the ground with great violence. He sustained very serious injuries and was removed to to the Altrincham hospital, where he died on Tuesday morning. The deoeased, who was very generally esteemed in the town leaves a widow and four children. The deceased was 35 years of age. An inquest was held on Thursday, at the Altrincham Hospital, before Mr. Dunstan, coroner, when it tran- spired that by the accident both the deceased's arms were fractured. After his admission into the hospital ae was delirious, and instead of keeping his arms— which had been set—still, he at frequent intervals would move them, and so prevented their healing This caused erysipelas to ensue, and knally blood poisoning. The jury returned the following verdict—. " That the deceased died from blood poisoning result- ing from erysipelas, the result of fractures, through a ladder upon which he was engaged at work having been accidentally knocked down by a cart, the horse attached to which took fright at a noise made by a handcart drawn toy some boys, the horse having been , left without in attendant, and the ladder insufficiently protected." The jury recommended that in future employers should be more careful in seeing after ouch I matters.

Councillor Mown, in supporting them, said Since the town's meeting one has come into contact with many people, and I coulees that I sim somewhat 'sur- prised at the amount of ignorance that is displayed as to the terms of the purchase of the Gas Works. We have all heard arguments against the purchase, but I am quite satisfied that we have not yet heard all the arguments in favour of it. There is one matter I should like to refer to, namely, the price of the mate. rial which. has been used. I refer to this now because it has been said again and again that last year was not a fair test to go by. All I have to say is that taking last year, when the price at which coal was purchased was the highest ever given by the Gas Company within 2s. per ton, and the price of 1872 and 1873, which I think is nearer the mark than the price of 1876, I think it will show a very much more favourable balance than the balance which we have taken, which Is £7,161. I have found this to be so convincing to those with whom I have spoken, that I felt it might be of use to mention it in the Council tonight. (Hear, hear.) If we deal ee ith the matter in this way, and sesame that the Gas Company for last year had been able to purchase their coals at the price they did in 1872 and 1873, instead of their profits being £7,161, they would have been £9,477. (Hear, hear.) If we deduct from that the perpetual annuides of £6 120, then we have left as a balance, which would have been at the disposal of the Corporation, a suns of £0,357, in- stead of £l,OOO. I mention this because I feel that we have at the present moment an opportunity of secur- ing what I conceive to be a very valuable property. I am satisfied that if we miss this opportunity we shall not have it again, I think, in my lifetime; so that any information that can be given to-night which will have a tendency to clear up any prejudices in the minds of the public, should be given uow. There is another view of the question that I think ought to be referred to, namely, the prospective view. That has been dealt with very clearly in the reports which have been issued, but I wieh to suggest another way of bringing out results- I think there can be no doubt on the minds of those who have studied the matter that within the next five years the whole of the £43,200 will have to be called up and spext in the extension of the works. I find that the produotive power will then be in round numbers 200,000,000 cubic feet per annum. If we take the Caine basis of calcula- tion, and work it out as a role of three sum, even at the price of coals for last year, which was exoeptionally high. that at the end, when the consumption amounts to 200,000 000 cubic feet we shall have a profit of Al ,035 per annum, from which we sh .11 hive to de- duct not only the £6,120 payable to the shareholders of the old company, but we shell have 4 per cent on the £43,000, which could be raised at 4 per cent. (Hear, bear.) And add these two figures together we get a total of payments on behalf of the company of £7,848. That is, taking almost the worst feature of it, that the profit widen will be left aveil tble for the Cor- poration when the production is 200,000,000 cubic feet per annum will be £4,187 per annum. And if we take it at the price which coal was bought at in the years 1872-3, instead of a profit of £4,187 it will leave avail- able to the Corporation a profit of £8,122 per annum surplus, after paying interest to shareholdere and bond- holder.. (Hear, hear.) That is, very riefly, as far as lam able to get at it, the result which will be due to -this Corporation; and I think it is only fair to the Gas Company and to the ratepayers at large, that this should he broadly stated and made known, that the public may form their own conclusions. I don't enter into the question of capitalizing, &c., but I think enough has been said to satisfy the people of even a larger town than Warrington that we have a chance of securing a property which will yield to the Corporation a revenue of £B,OOO a year. div.p: NOTES.

The number of dogs and fowls lately poisoned in and around Widnes is just now attracting consider- able attention, and exciting some alarm amongst the owners of such domestic favourites. At Simms' Cross, within a very short period, two persons have lost in this way a total of 36 fowls all of considerable value. Several dogs have been similarly destroyed. This cowardly and detestable crime deserves prompt discovery and universal reprobation. If the rascally perpetrator of the outrage is found to infest the vicinity of Widnes, it is to be hoped that stringent measures will be adopted to reform him.

The wit and wisdom of the Runcorn Commis- sioners ever affords merriment or instruction to those who are so happy as to peruse the story of their labours in the public service. It is a little unkind of these gentlemen, however, to complain of the publicity which enables their neighbours to partici- pate in the frolic effervescence of their high animal spirits, or in that sententious—what did Mr. Grant Duff call it when lately in Liverpool P—oh ! " quintessence " of local statesmanship, by which their proceedings are usually signalised. At their last meeting it seems that Mr. P. Speakman be- sought the reporters to "take no notes of any 'childish remarks' which might be made at the Board, for they didn't mean anything." Now, one has a great respect for the intellectual capacity of our purveyors of news, but to insist on these gentlemen being always able to discriminate in the matter of oratorical chiclishness is to exact too much. It would simplify the matter if the " childishness " were eliminated by the Com- missioners themselves. Mr. Collier spoke out on the occasion boldly like a man—and a Runcorn Commissioner. "The newspapers," he said, "tell some abominable lies." "I scarcely ever read their reports "—he continued—" There is always some- thing wrong whenever my name is mentioned. Go straightforward about your work, and never mind the newspapers ! " This is really very good advice, and cannot be too widely accepted by " Improve- ment Commissioners" of every description, but it cannot escape Mr. Collier's sagacity that if every- body besides himself scarcely ever read a newspaper report, these words of wisdom of his might have wasted their sweetness on the desert air of the com- mittee room. Mr. Collier received capital support from the Chairman when he said that "If they did their duty they needn't fear the reporters" ! "Nor any other man, Mr. Chairman." It is equally true, however, that if the Press does its duty, it needn't fear even the Runcorn Commissioners.

The combination of the characters of Mars aud Apollo is by no means uncommon in Ireland, and one is pleased to see that the "Irish Duke"—. meaning the Royal "Irish Duke," is exercising his musical as well as his martial accomplishments in Dublin. We read that the Duke of Connaught took part in a musical entertainment at the Dublin Bar- racks on Friday night, playing the piano accom- paniment for the two items in the programme. One would like to hear of this Queen's son ooming out into the open, and being found like his brother of Edin- burgh, comfortably fiddling at a public concert. In this country there is no political sphere for scions of the reigning House, but as an alternative they have "the music of the spheres," and Wagner. The Duke of Edinburgh, who is said to be more than an amateur player on the violin, seems to have discerned a certain way to popular admiration, for, as Edwin Waugh in one of his Lancashire songs has it— "A mon 'at plays the fiddle weel Should never awse to dee." How potent is that "one touch of nature."

The gentlemen of Cheshire who, in the hunting season, blaze over their Cheshire acres in ceremonial scarlet after the "little game," which the farmer feeds with so much delight and liberality, pay a not in- considerable price for the joys of Nimrod. They do not pay more, perhaps, than their pinked and leathered confreres in the field in other counties, but their perils being nearer home are more impressive. Scarcely a week passes during the hunting season that some farmer's friend doesn't fracture his ribs, or break his collar bone, or his arm, or his legs in Pursuit of the pleasures of the chase. These plea- sures must be very real and very seductive, for they do not fascinate merely the owners of the acres and the friendly agriculturist who farms them, but they attract irresistably gentlemen from Manchester and Liverpool, who grow no turnips ,of their own, and have no smiling tenants to give them jovial wel- come. One is sincerely sorry to see that this dan- gerous taste has just resulted fatally in the case of a gentleman named Finley, a bootmaker from King. street, Manchester, who, with his son and some friends were hunting with the Cheshire Hounds near Wrenbury. The unfortunate man, who was thrown from his horse, died last Saturday of concussion of the brain! Hunting in Cheshire, as elsewhere, is clearly as perilous as it is expensive. It is almost needless to say that these dismil possibilities of English sport happen in every rank of hunting society. I see that a Sheffield correspondent states that Lady Theodora Grosvenor has sustained a bad fall while hunting with Lord Wolverton's blood- hounds. Her horse slipped at a tree fence and threw her heavily, after which the animal ran away. Her Ladyship was much shaken and bruised. Speaking seriously, the British fanner mud regard these "moving accidents" in the hunting field with curiously mingled feelings.

The reformatory plaister seems somewhat out of proportion with what one may call the troublesome pimple of j uvenile bellringing. However, reformatories are the places to which mischievous young shavers are to be sent, who ring door bells to the annoyance of peaceful residents. Perhaps this threat made use of by Mr. Joynson, the chairman of the Bench of magistrates, to the terrible boy who appeared be" fore him at the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday, for this offence, will have the effect of stopping this exasperating juvenile recreation. It is the trifling yet multifarious worries of life that bother us even more than trouble of a larger growth. The mosquito can make himself in- tolerable, and I trust that Mr. Joynson's warning will appeal to the business and bosoms—or shall I say business and corduroys of the little boys whom it may concern.

This club held its first conversszione of the season at the Town Hall on Monday; the entire suite of rooms having been, through the Mayor's kindness, thrown open to the company. Houghton Hague exhibited the clever study, in "black and white," of his picture of "The Chimney Corner" and its inmates, intended for an illustration of Mr. Waugh's forth- coming volume. Rogers, of London, addressed a large and enthusiastic meeting in the Town Hall, Newcastle- on-Tyne, on the disestablishment and disendowment of the Church of England. Mr. Joseph Cowen, M P., presided; and in opening the meeting he said there had been some talk the last two or three years about a Liberal reaction, but he had not been able to see it until the last week, when the school board election in London showed, in his opinion, that the reaction had really begun. Mr. Cowen further stated at the close of the meeting that he did not believe that the Liberal party were so much in favour of the church as some people supposed. They remembered how they had been treated by the clergy in the last election. When the Liberals got again into power, the day on which religious equality would be proclaimed in this country might not be so far off as some people imagined. The meeting was not the largest meeting that had been held in the hall, as it was not filled, but it was one of the most enthusiastio.

MR. BRIGHT AT BIRMINGHAM. On Monday evening Mr. Bright addressed a large and enthusiastic meeting in the Town Hall, at Bir- mingham, on the Eastern Question. Mr. Bright briefly recapitulated the principal events of the past year, and inquired why war was considered imminent, although every Government in Europe was in favour of perice. The answer was, because England was de- termined by means of Turkey to keep the Russian ships of war out of the Mediterranean. He ridiculed the idea of there being any danger to English interests in the presence of a Russian navy in that sea. The vessels of other nations were permitted there, and the skies would not fall if Russia was admitted. She was 'nein led by frost from passing from the Baltic during half the year, and throughout the whole year from passing the Dardanelles, because Turkey held the keys' for England. If England were in such a position the unanimous voice of the nation would claim the right for her vessels to enter the Mediterrean. He urged that Great Britain should join Russia in urging re- forms on Tnrkey. and if she could not do that let her stand aside. Ref erring to the Conference, he said Lord Salisbury's home policy had been marked by arrogance and nnwisdom, but his Indian policy by justice and humanity. He hoped that at Constantinople his ability and justice would have fair play, and that he would do himself and his country honour by the duty he had undertaken.

div.head: AFFAIRS IN THE EAST
div.p: AFFAIRS IN THE EAST

Eastern affairs, although making little visible progress, cannot be fairly said to "drag their slow length along," for they are certainly culminating in the great Con- ference which will immediately assemble in Constantinople, the troublous capital where Lord Salisbury has at length arrived. The telegrams of the past week have made it clearer than ever that England has not found a single ally in Europe willing to stake a man or a pound in the maintenance of what is still called— with very dismal humour— "the integrity of Turkey." Whatever therefore may happen to what Mr. Carlyle designates as "the un- speakable Turk," employment will scarcely be found for the big fleet in Basika Bay, and the oriental fire-eater at Guildhall, who menaced Russia with quite a number of campaigns to be equipped and paid for by the English people, will have his braggart labour for his pains. If it were not the merest trifle, in comparison with the ap- palling and bloody issues to which "pretty Fanny's way" might have committed the country, it would be curious to note the way in which the Premier will escape the extraordinary dilemma in which his frightful recklessness has placed his Cabinet. In one of the comedies of Sheridan, certain conspirators swear fealty to each other on their knees, and a difficulty arises in the absence of a stage direction—as to how they will resume their normal posi- tion. A. critic who is present suggests that it would add interest to the situation if they could be made to leave the stage still kneel- ing. If Lord Beaconsfield and his Cabinet supporters of the "unspeakable Turk" could appropriately disappear from the view of the country in this penitential attitude, poetical justice would possibly be satisfied.

A town meeting, presided over by the Mayor, was held at Manchester to consider the Eastern Question, A resolution was passed in favour of England acting in concert with the European powers, and especially with Russia, to secure the release of the oppreisad provinces from the direct rule of the Turk and appointing delegates to the National Conference, which is to assemble on Friday.

Prince Bismarck has made a speech at a Parlia- mentary dinner which he gave on Friday. He laid stress upon the neutral attitude which Germany would assume in the event of war, and also upon her friendly relations with Austria. If hostilities occurred he thought that they ought to be localised, and that England ought not to isolate herself from the other Powers, and engage in a quarrel with Russia. He hoped at all events that she would not openly wage war against that Power, but at most carry on opera- tions indirectly, as Russia had in Servia.

Mr. Hopwood, M.P., in the course of a speech delivered on Saturday, near Rochdale, expressed his conviction that England would never _go to war to support the domination of Turkey in Europe. The people of this country had spoken out unmistakably on the subject, and need be under no apprehension. Lord Beaconsfield dare not drag them into war.

Prince Bismarck, replying to a question in the Ger- man Parliament on Tuesday, repeated in effect what he had said on the European crisis in his speech at the Parliamentary dinner, except that he was more ex- plicit as to the triple alliance. He assured the Parlia- ment that the three Emperors' alliance exists in its full integrity, but he added that this did not in the least preclude cordial friendship with England, the friendly relationship with which, as established by long tradition, Germany values as highly as the ..t with any other nation.

On his way he was enthusiastically received by the in- habitants of Moscow, and entertained by Prince Dol- goroukyi. The Prince proposed the health of the Grand Duke, and said in concluding his speed), "It is a great honour for me that the commander of the Russian army starts from my house to commence his military achievements."

THE CENTURY;
No. VI.—SECOND PART.
IRELAND.*

Wool, was not the only commodity put under restriction. There is little doubt that numerous trades would have taken deep root in Ireland if they had not been ruth- lessly suppressed. Smuggling was exalted to a virtue. Persons of all ranks in Ireland were principals or accomplices in smuggling. "Distinctions of creed,' says Mr. Fronde, "were obliterated, and resistance to law became a bond of union between Catholic and Protestant, Irish Celt and English colonist, from the great landlord whose sheep roamed in thousands over the Cork mountains, to the guager who, with con- veniently blinded eyes, passed the wool packs through the Custom House as butter barrels, from the magistrate whose cellars were filled with claret on the return voyage of the smuggling craft, to the judge on the bench who dismissed as frivolous and vexatious the various cup which came before the Courts to be tried. But bad as were the trading imports they were nothing compared with the religious and social disabilities under which the people groaned. A nation can endure poverty, but unless its spirit is utterly crushed it cannot live under persecution and tyranny. It is horrible to read of the penalties imposed upon our fellow subjects. Sydney Smith during his gallant agitation in favour of Catholic Emancipation analyses in the Edinburgh Review, the various enact- ments for the suppression of Romanisna, and alludes to the penalties imposed upon believers of the Romish creed, Mr. Lecky has ably summarised these, and although somewhat lengthy we cannot refrain from quoting him, "While the prosperity of the Protestants was being crushed by the com- mercial laws, the Catholics were suffering under the penal code—a code which Burke described as 'well digested and well dis- posed in all its parts, a machine of wise and elaborate contrivance, and as well fitted for the oppression, impoverishment, and degre- dation of a people, and the debasement in them of human nature itself, as ever pro- ceeded from the perverted ingenuity of man.' The code excluded the Catholics from the Parliament, from the magistracy, from the Corporations, from the University, from the bench and from the bar, from the right of voting at parliamentary elections or at vestries, of acting as constables, as sheriffs, or as jurymen, or serving in the army or navy, of becoming solicitors, or even holding the position of gamekeeper or watchman. They prohibited them from be- coming schoolmasters, ushers, or private tutors; or from sending their children abroad to receive the Catholic e•ducation they were iefused at home. They offered an annuity (of £3O) to every priest who would forsake his creed, pronounced a sentence of exile against the whole hierarchy, and restricted the right of celebrating mass to registered priests, whose number was not to be re- newed. 2he Catholics could not buy land, or inherit or reef ive it as a gift from Pro- testants, or hold life annuities or leases for more than 31 years, or any lease on such terms that the profits of the land exceeded one- third of the rent. A Catholic, except in the linen trade, could have no more than two apprentices. He could not have a horse of the value of more than £5, and any Pro- testant on giving him £5 might take his horse. He was compelled to pay double to the militia. In case of war with a Catholic Power he was obliged to reimburse the damage done by the enemy's privateers. To convert a Protestant to Cotholicism was a capital offence. No Catholic might merry a Protestant. (The priests are now retaliating and will not permit a 'mixed' marriage of one of their communion with a 'heretic' —so-called. 7 his is as shameful an act of tyrrany as that we are denouncing.) A Catholic landowner might not bequeath his land as he pleases. It was divided equally I amongst his children, unless the eldest son became a Protestant, in which case the parent became simply a life tenant, and lost all power of selling or mortgaging it. If a Catholic's wife abandoned her husband's religion she was immediately free from his control, and the Chancellor could assign her a certain proportion of her husband's pro- perty. If his child, however young, pro- fessed itself a Protestant, it was taken from its father's care, and the Chancellor could assign it a portion of its father's property. No Catholic could be guardian to his own children." There were broadly speaking, but three sects in Ireland—Episcopalians, Presbyterians, and Roman Catholics. The first had all the privileges, the other two shared the disabilities. If an able man arose among the Presbyterians, he at once found himself shut out by the test from the path of honor. But if he were a Catholic he was excluded by the penal laws from every field of ambition, and from almost every possi- bility of acquiring influence or wealth. One wonders how the people could have endured the strain so long. Yet the Catholics were loyal to the Crown, and in the rebellion of 1715 and 1745 remained passive, and the priests warned the Government of the plots I of the Pretender. liallum points out that when the American Colonies had revolted against England, and at a time when the Presbyterians were profoundly disaffected, the Catholics were ardently loyal. We shall have to trace the agitation which resulted in the complete abolition of these wrongs, and the restoration of our Catholic fellow-subjects to a just position in the commonwealth.

A THEATRE BURNT AT BROOKLYN. GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. A terrible accident has occurred at Brooklyn. The Brooklyn Theatre caught fire on Tuesday nivht just before the close of the performance. About eOO per. sans were present. Of these 300 are believed to have perished. The great loss of life appears to have been principally caused by the balustrade of the gallery staircase giving way while the audience were hurriedly escaping. A heaP of more than 203 bodies was found so charred as to be hardly recognisable. - FRANCE. RESIGNATION OF THE MINISTRY. At a Cabinet Council on Saturday, the whole of the French Ministers placed their resignations in the hands of Marshall MscMahon, owing to the defeats recently sustained by M. Dufaure. The Marshall urged them, but to no pu, pose, to reconsider their determination. In the Chamber on eaturday, the Gevarnment withdrew the Funeral Honours Bill, and accepted an order of the day, which was carried by a large majority, recognising the principles of liberty of conscience and the equality of ciVzens in the eyes of the law. • A WARNING TO HOLDERS OF OUT-DOOR LICENSES. Hy. Howl, provision dealer and beerseller, 13. Pier- point-street, was charged with that he being the holder of an excise license to sell beer to 12:e consumed off the premises, did unlawfully and knowing permit a certain quantity of beer to be drunk on the said pre- mises. Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant. Ser. geant Berry stated that in accordaace with instructions received from the Chief Conetab,e, he and P.C. Wor• rall went to Pierpoint-street, off Bewsey road, in plain clothes. They got there about half-past six in the morning, and secreted themselves. About nine o'clock three men, apparently plasterers, went into the pas- sage adjoining defendant's house. Each man was supplied with a jag out of which he drank. From that time to a quarter to two o'clock this conduct was re- peated by several persona who came to the shop and drank beer. The p dice then appeared upon the scene and informed defendant's wife that they had been watching what was going on. Mr. Moore stated that if the law had been broken it had not been broken tentionallv. The defendant had given strict instruc- tions to his wife and servants not to allow beer to be consumed on the premiseq. The Bench then retired from court to consider their decision. On their return the Mayor said they had had no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that there had been a breach of the law. The defendant had rendered himself liable to a Penalty of £lO. However, as that was the defendant's first offence, he would be fined 4Cre and costs. Robert Ivens. Thomas Morgan, Peter Briars, William Parry, and Hugh Donnelly were then charged with aiding and abetting the defendant Howl—lvers and Morgan were ordered to pay c-sts, and Parry and Donnelly were fined ss. and costs each.
